title: Hezekiah's Deliverance
overview: 2 Chronicles 32 recounts the dramatic siege of Jerusalem by Sennacherib, king of Assyria, during the reign of Hezekiah. The chapter highlights Hezekiah’s strategic preparations, including fortifying the city and securing water supplies, and his reliance on God for deliverance. Despite Assyria’s threats and blasphemies against the God of Israel, Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah pray earnestly, resulting in divine intervention that defeats the Assyrian army. The chapter also records Hezekiah’s later illness, his pride, and subsequent humility, emphasizing the importance of faithfulness and dependence on God. This chapter serves as a powerful testimony to God’s protection of His people and the consequences of pride, fitting within the broader narrative of Judah’s kings and God’s covenantal faithfulness.
structure:
**Verses 1-8: The Threat and Preparations.** The chapter opens with Sennacherib’s invasion and Hezekiah’s response, including military and infrastructural preparations and a rallying speech to encourage courage and trust in God.

**Verses 9-19: Assyrian Taunts and Psychological Warfare.** Sennacherib’s servants send messages to intimidate Jerusalem’s inhabitants, mocking their trust in God and Hezekiah’s reforms, attempting to undermine their faith and morale.

**Verses 20-23: Divine Deliverance.** Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and God sends an angel who annihilates the Assyrian army, forcing Sennacherib to retreat in disgrace, culminating in his assassination.

**Verses 24-26: Hezekiah’s Illness and Pride.** Hezekiah falls gravely ill, prays to God, and receives a sign of healing, but later his heart is lifted up in pride, bringing God’s wrath upon him and Judah.

**Verses 27-31: Hezekiah’s Wealth and Prosperity.** The chapter concludes with a description of Hezekiah’s riches, fortifications, and prosperity, but also notes God’s testing of his heart through Babylonian envoys.

**Verses 32-33: Conclusion and Death of Hezekiah.** The final verses reference additional records of Hezekiah’s reign and his honorable burial, marking the end of his faithful kingship.

keyVerses.text: Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is with him: for there be more with us than with him: With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
keyVerses.significance: These verses emphasize the central theological truth of the chapter: trust in God over human strength. Hezekiah’s encouragement reveals the source of true courage and victory, underscoring God’s sovereignty in battle and the importance of faith in divine help.

keyVerses.text: And for this cause Hezekiah the king, and the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, prayed and cried to heaven. And the LORD sent an angel, which cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned with shame of face to his own land. And when he was come into the house of his god, they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword.
keyVerses.significance: This passage highlights the power of prayer and God’s miraculous intervention on behalf of His people. It demonstrates that God actively defends His covenant community and judges the proud oppressors, fulfilling His promises of protection.

keyVerses.text: But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem. Notwithstanding Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the LORD came not upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
keyVerses.significance: These verses reveal the danger of pride even after experiencing God’s blessings and deliverance. Hezekiah’s humility after being corrected shows the necessity of repentance and dependence on God to avoid judgment.

keyVerses.text: Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
keyVerses.significance: This verse introduces the theme of testing and divine sovereignty in the affairs of kings. God’s allowing Hezekiah to be tested reveals the importance of the king’s heart and faithfulness, foreshadowing future challenges for Judah.

characters.name: Hezekiah
characters.description: King of Judah who leads the defense against Assyria by fortifying Jerusalem and encouraging his people to trust God. He is a model of faith and prayer but also experiences pride and humility, illustrating the complexities of godly leadership.

characters.name: Sennacherib
characters.description: King of Assyria who invades Judah and mocks the God of Israel in an attempt to intimidate Jerusalem. His defeat by divine intervention demonstrates God's power over earthly empires.

characters.name: Isaiah
characters.description: The prophet who supports Hezekiah through prayer and counsel, representing God’s prophetic voice and intercession during the crisis.

characters.name: The LORD God
characters.description: The sovereign God of Israel who defends His people, answers prayer, and executes judgment on Assyria, affirming His covenant faithfulness and power.

themes.description: The chapter vividly portrays God’s intervention to save Jerusalem from Assyria, reinforcing the biblical theme that God protects His covenant people against overwhelming odds.
Hezekiah’s exhortation to be strong and courageous highlights the necessity of faith in God’s power rather than human strength, a recurring biblical principle.
Hezekiah’s experience with pride and subsequent humility teaches the dangers of self-exaltation and the need for repentance to maintain God’s favor.
The collaboration between Hezekiah and Isaiah in prayer underscores the importance of seeking God’s guidance and intervention through prophetic ministry.

historicalContext: This chapter is set in the late 8th century BC during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah, a period marked by Assyrian expansion under Sennacherib. Jerusalem, located in the hill country of Judah, was a fortified city vulnerable to siege warfare. The Assyrian empire was the dominant military power in the ancient Near East, known for brutal campaigns and deportations. Hezekiah’s reforms, including centralizing worship in Jerusalem and removing high places, challenged Assyrian influence and provoked their invasion. The political context involved complex alliances and threats, with Judah caught between Assyria and Babylon. The chapter reflects the geopolitical realities and religious tensions of the time, emphasizing reliance on God amid external threats.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God's sovereign providence in delivering His people, viewing Hezekiah’s faith and prayer as examples of trusting God’s covenant promises. The defeat of Assyria is seen as a demonstration of God’s power over nations and idolatry.

Dispensationalists highlight the literal historical fulfillment of God’s protection of Israel and the prophetic significance of Hezekiah’s reign as part of God’s unfolding plan for Israel, with the Assyrian invasion foreshadowing future eschatological conflicts.

Early church interpreters often saw Hezekiah’s deliverance as typological of Christ’s victory over evil, with the angelic destruction of Assyria prefiguring spiritual warfare and God’s ultimate triumph over Satan.

application: Trust God in the face of overwhelming challenges rather than relying solely on human strength or resources.
Prepare diligently and wisely while maintaining faith that God ultimately controls the outcome.
Respond to God’s blessings with humility to avoid the pitfalls of pride and self-exaltation.
Engage in earnest prayer and seek godly counsel during times of crisis.
Recognize that God tests our hearts through circumstances to reveal our true faith and dependence on Him.
Encourage others with words of faith and courage grounded in God’s promises.
conclusion: 2 Chronicles 32 stands as a powerful testament to God’s faithfulness in delivering His people when they trust and obey Him. Hezekiah’s leadership, marked by practical preparation and spiritual reliance, models godly courage. The chapter also warns against pride, emphasizing humility and repentance. Through prayer and divine intervention, God demonstrates His sovereignty over nations and idols, encouraging believers to place their confidence in Him alone. This chapter continues to inspire faith, courage, and dependence on God’s providence in the face of adversity.

outline.heading: The Assyrian Threat and Hezekiah’s Preparations

outline.heading: Assyrian Taunts Against Jerusalem
outline.description: Sennacherib’s servants send messages to intimidate Jerusalem’s inhabitants, mocking their faith and Hezekiah’s reforms, attempting to weaken their resolve.

outline.heading: Prayer and Divine Deliverance
outline.description: Hezekiah and Isaiah pray for God’s intervention, resulting in an angel destroying the Assyrian army and Sennacherib’s humiliating retreat and death.

outline.heading: Hezekiah’s Illness, Pride, and Humility
outline.description: Hezekiah’s sickness and healing sign are followed by his pride, which brings God’s wrath; however, his humility averts further judgment.

outline.heading: Hezekiah’s Wealth, Prosperity, and Testing
outline.description: The king’s riches and fortifications grow, but God tests his heart through the visit of Babylonian envoys, revealing the ongoing spiritual challenges.

outline.description: The chapter closes with a reference to additional records of Hezekiah’s reign and his honorable burial, marking the end of his faithful leadership.
